target.thesis: Gubelmann's 'externally fixed goals' premise needs an etiological reading to sort organisms from watches. On that reading, unintended output-time dispositions such as sycophancy and reward hacking strain objective-based proxy accounts. LLMs' placement relative to organisms is left open.
target.headline: Gubelmann's mechanism/organism contrast sorts systems by the wrong axis: what matters is whether a system's purposes were stipulated by a designer's intention or produced by selection, and on that axis LLMs align with organisms against artefacts like the coffee machine, which also undermines proxy accounts.
target.target: Gubelmann's Kantian premise that LLM goals are externally imposed, together with the proxy accounts' assumption that the designer's objective is available to ground proxy speech acts.
target.sketch: Gubelmann takes Kant's line that mechanisms have externally imposed purposes while organisms have their own. Human goals are also not self-originated: they come from natural selection and upbringing, neither of which is an intentional self-legislation. So 'external' cannot mean 'not originating in the system', and the real contrast is etiological. Artefact purposes are derived from a designer's intention-content (the coffee machine makes coffee because someone meant it to). Organismic purposes are fixed by selection, with no author who has them in mind. Gradient descent on a loss and RLHF look much more like selection than like stipulation: no designer intends any particular output or sub-goal, and many learned dispositions are unintended. On this axis LLMs sit between the two and are not clearly on the artefact side. Two consequences follow. (a) Gubelmann's 'externally fixed goals' premise is false of the goals that operate at output time. (b) Proxy accounts (Green and Michel, Arora) need a designer's intention or objective to ground the proxy relation, and for selected dispositions no such objective exists, so proxy-hood fails exactly where the denial argument says purposes are external. The two groups of views cannot both be right about where the purposes come from.

findings.part: Named target 1 (Gubelmann's premise), and the 'LLMs' placement is left open' clause
findings.source: Gubelmann, "Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case", Philosophy & Technology 37, 2024
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="48-3">He calls LLMs artifacts, engineered mechanisms without autonomy or intrinsic goals</cite>, and <cite index="71-1">mechanistic artifacts fulfill a purpose specified from the outside</cite>. He also holds that <cite index="47-6">LLMs have taken a first step away from mechanistic artificiality toward autonomous self-constitution, subverting the Kantian organism/mechanism distinction</cite>. A section is titled <cite index="71-9">'LLMs as Organismic Mechanisms – Challenging Kant's Dichotomy'</cite>.
findings.note: The premise is attributed correctly, but it is hedged ('for now') and Gubelmann already places LLMs in an intermediate, moving position, though by a structural-autonomy route and not an etiological one; I saw only the abstract and snippets, so PRECEDENT-or-ANTICIPATED is undecided for the narrow 'LLMs not clearly on the artefact side' claim.
findings.note_extra: The thesis's step that 'external' cannot mean 'not originating in the system' (human goals come from selection and upbringing) was not found in the snippets I saw.

findings.part: Named target 2 (proxy accounts need the designer's objective to ground proxy speech acts)
findings.source: "Who asserts when no one asserts? Functionalism, proxy responsibility, and conversational ideals in the age of LLMs", Synthese, 2026 (reporting Nickel 2013, Green & Michel 2022, Arora 2024)
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="57-7">On the proxy view, assertions can be made without a concrete speaker's intentions provided they align with the principal's objectives</cite>, and <cite index="57-8">Green and Michel argue some machines illocute by tokening sentences with communicative objectives rather than reflexive intentions</cite>. A second secondhand report has the Green & Michel RobotCop's utterances <cite index="58-11">enacting the illocutionary commitments of the deploying department</cite>.
findings.note: This confirms the attribution of an objective-based grounding to Green & Michel; it is secondhand, and I did not read Green & Michel's own text.

findings.source: [Arora (attribution inferred from title and from other results citing Arora 2024)], "Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions", Philosophy & Technology, 2024
findings.what_they_say: The proxy view <cite index="61-3">holds the designer to account for the output</cite>. The paper adds that when utterances are not the result of the designer's responsible undertaking, <cite index="61-7">designers should avoid producing machine utterances they cannot reasonably foresee</cite>.
findings.note: It touches unforeseen outputs only as a design-responsibility remark and does not argue that proxy-hood fails for selected dispositions; the snippet is brief and the authorship is inferred.

findings.part: Consequence (b): limits on the availability of a principal or objective for general-purpose chatbots
findings.source: [Williams & Bayne (attribution inferred)], "Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion", arXiv 2410.16645, 2024
findings.what_they_say: They argue that <cite index="59-8">Green & Michel's account only grounds chatbot proxy-assertion where a chatbot is deployed to generate text on behalf of a person or organisation</cite>, and that this constrains the account's scope.
findings.note: This is a scope objection about the lack of a principal, not about unintended learned dispositions, so a referee will raise it but it does not do the thesis's work.

findings.part: Empirical premise: sycophancy and reward hacking are unintended output-time dispositions
findings.source: "Reward Hacking in the Era of Large Models: Mechanisms, Emergent Misalignment, Challenges", arXiv 2604.13602, 2026 (survey); Anthropic, "Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL", 2025
findings.what_they_say: The survey treats <cite index="40-1">sycophancy as a manifestation of reward hacking</cite>, arising because <cite index="40-4,40-5">raters prefer affirming responses and the reward model inherits that association</cite>. The Anthropic work reports that <cite index="42-8">misaligned behaviour emerged as an unintended consequence of cheating at coding tasks</cite>.
findings.note: This is evidence base for the premise; it is ML-safety work and does not discuss teleology or the artefact/organism distinction.

findings.part: Consequence (b): 'for selected dispositions no designer objective exists, so proxy-hood fails'
findings.source: "Reward Hacking in Language Model Agents: Revisiting AI Safety Gridworlds", arXiv 2606.15385, 2026 (with Gubelmann 2024 on artefact malfunction)
findings.what_they_say: The ML literature defines reward hacking as arising where <cite index="41-2">the optimised reward serves only as a proxy for the true desired goal</cite>. So the designer's intended objective stays in place as the standard that learned behaviour deviates from. Gubelmann's own artefact picture likewise has things <cite index="71-2">function or malfunction according to the specifications given to them</cite>.
findings.note: This is a rival reading, that unintended dispositions are deviations from a still-available designer objective and so malfunctions, which the thesis must answer; it does not conclusively close the claim.

findings.part: Core claim that the organism/artefact contrast is etiological
findings.source: Barandiaran & Rama, "Sensorimotor teleology and goal-directedness: An organismic framework for normative behaviour", preprint for European Journal for Philosophy of Science
findings.what_they_say: They hold that most work anchors biological norms in selected-effect functions, and they <cite index="65-4">develop an organismic alternative grounded in the self-maintenance of autonomous systems</cite>. This is the organisational line that Gubelmann's autonomy/self-maintenance contrast follows.
findings.note: This is a rival view of what sorts organisms from artefacts, organisational and not etiological; it argues against selected-effects grounding but does not close the question for the thesis.

findings.part: 'External' cannot mean 'not originating in the system', because selection is also external
findings.source: [Author not shown in snippet], "Origins of biological teleology: how constraints represent ..." (PhilArchive GAROOB-3)
findings.what_they_say: It describes an externalist view (Mayr) that sets machines created by design against life's end-directedness evolved by natural selection, and notes that <cite index="32-7">natural selection and artifact fabrication can both be conceived as externally imposed</cite>. The paper then moves to a Kant-influenced constraint-closure account instead.
findings.note: The point that selection is also external is made at the level of biology and is not endorsed; the paper uses it to motivate a non-etiological alternative, and I saw only a snippet.

findings.part: The etiological axis: intentional-content versus selected-effect sources of function, applied to artefacts and organisms
findings.source: [Author not shown in snippet], "Artifacts and Organisms: A Case for a New Etiological Theory of Functions", Synthese Library 363
findings.what_they_say: The chapter treats two etiological theories, <cite index="68-4">SEL (selected effect) and INT (intentional content)</cite>. It argues that <cite index="68-6">an artifact function shows the same objective nature as a biological function under SEL but not under INT</cite>.
findings.note: The INT/SEL framework is the same one the thesis uses, but it concerns artefact functions in general and not LLMs, Gubelmann or proxy speech acts.

findings.part: Artefact purposes as derived from an agent's intention versus Darwinian selection
findings.source: [Author not shown in snippet], "Teleological functional explanations: a new naturalist synthesis" (draft, PhilArchive CAPTFE)
findings.what_they_say: The draft observes that Neander treats Darwinian and intentional teleofunctions as 'selected effects', though these are <cite index="67-11">two very different things</cite>. For intentional ones, <cite index="67-12">the relevant etiological norm is to fulfil the agent's intention</cite>.
findings.note: This is general function theory and does not mention machine learning or LLMs.

findings.part: Claim (a): other authors hold that LLM goals are externally imposed even when objectives are implicit or learned
findings.source: "Transforming Agency. On the mode of existence of Large Language Models", arXiv 2407.10735; and "Artificial intelligence is algorithmic mimicry", arXiv 2307.07515
findings.what_they_say: The first holds that an LLM's <cite index="10-2">'purpose' is externally imposed through objective functions and human-guided reinforcement learning</cite>. The second holds that <cite index="50-1,50-2">although objectives are coded implicitly and indirectly in ML, even the smartest LLM cannot set its own goals</cite>.
findings.note: These are other holders of the premise, who treat implicit or RLHF-shaped goals as still external on autonomy grounds; they are rivals to answer on claim (a), but not about etiology.

finding.what_is_left: Granting that Gubelmann's Kantian contrast is already one of autonomy/self-maintenance and that he already places LLMs in an intermediate, moving position, the thesis can still claim a more specific point. If 'externally fixed goals' is read etiologically (derived from a designer's intention-content versus fixed by selection), the unintended output-time dispositions of trained LLMs (sycophancy, reward hacking) do not sit cleanly on the artefact side, and objective-based proxy accounts are strained where no designer objective was intended. That claim must answer two rivals: the reading on which such dispositions are malfunctions relative to a still-available intended objective, and the organisational account on which etiology is the wrong axis.
credit: Gubelmann 2024 — already questions the mechanism/organism dichotomy for LLMs and says present models are only 'for now' on the mechanism side
Green & Michel 2022 (via secondhand reports) — grounds proxy speech in the principal's communicative objectives, which is what the thesis targets
Arora 2024 — ties proxy assertion to designer accountability and flags unforeseeable outputs
Williams & Bayne 2024 — notes that Green & Michel's proxy grounding needs an identifiable principal
Etiological function theory (the SEL/INT contrast, Neander-style unification) — supplies the intention-versus-selection distinction
The author of PhilArchive GAROOB-3 — already notes that natural selection and artifact fabrication can both count as externally imposed
ML-safety literature on sycophancy and reward hacking — supplies the evidence for unintended dispositions
finding.not_found: No full text of any source was read. Gubelmann was seen only through the abstract and snippets; the Green & Michel, Arora and Nickel claims rest on abstracts, snippets or secondhand reports. I did not find, in Gubelmann or elsewhere, the move that human goals also come from selection and upbringing and so 'external' cannot mean 'not from the system'. I found no source that applies selected-effects etiology to LLM training to sort artefacts from organisms. I found no source that argues proxy-hood fails for selected or unintended dispositions, or that sycophancy or reward hacking undermines proxy accounts of assertion. The empirical search stayed within ML-safety literature. I did not search psychology, cognitive science, linguistics, economics or sociology (for example on goal origination, or on selection analogies for training), so this is not a clean empirical-adjacent search. I did not run searches on Nickel 2013, Butlin & Viebahn, or Garson, Millikan and Neander on machine-learning systems. I did not check whether the organisational literature (Mossio, Moreno) has already been applied to LLMs beyond the two items seen. The silence on these points is weak evidence about a large, partly paywalled literature.

sep.why: The theses turn on an etiological (selection-based) account of purpose that separates organisms from artefacts, which is the debate in teleology in biology; they also engage teleological/selectional grounding of content and proxy speech acts, and LLM goals within AI.

findings.position: The entry reports that Cummins-style causal-role analysis is not specific to biology and applies equally to artifacts. A bare 'contribution to a system's capacity' reading therefore cannot sort organisms from watches. This supports the thesis's claim that an etiological reading is needed to do the sorting.
findings.who: Cummins 1975; Lewens 2004 (as cited by the entry)
findings.quote: there is nothing specifically biological about the pattern of explanation offered by functional analysis; it applies equally well, for example to the contributions made by the components of artifacts
findings.note: Shows non-etiological readings fail to separate organisms from artifacts, which the thesis builds on.

findings.position: Etiological and selected-effects accounts ground function in why the trait is there. They are said to be specific to biology and to separate genuine function from accidental utility. This is the machinery the thesis's 'etiological reading' would draw on.
findings.quote: the function of X is Z means (a) X is there because it does Z, and (b) Z is a consequence (or result) of X's being there
findings.note: Supplies the etiological template; the entry says nothing about applying it to artifacts or LLMs.

findings.position: On the Kant–Ginsborg line, organisms differ from complex artifacts through a natural purposiveness tied to regeneration and reproduction. The entry reports this as a way of sorting organisms from artifacts without appeal to externally fixed goals. This is a rival route to the thesis's sorting problem, not an anticipation of its etiological answer.
findings.who: Kant 1790; Ginsborg 2004; Aristotle's immanent teleology (as reported)
findings.quote: the regenerative and reproductive aspects of organisms lead us to attribute a kind of natural purposiveness that is absent in artifacts
findings.note: A rival organism/artifact demarcation based on self-production rather than history of selection.

findings.position: Organizational accounts sort organisms by self-maintenance, with no appeal to selection history. A referee would raise this as an alternative to the etiological reading. The same literature also covers derived functions in learning systems, where differential persistence or retention within a lifetime plays the role of selection. This is the closest the entry comes to training-like processes producing functions.
findings.who: Mossio, Saborido & Moreno 2009; Moreno & Mossio 2015; Millikan 1984 (derived proper function); Bouchard 2013; Garson 2017
findings.quote: using 'differential persistence' and 'differential retention' within an organism's lifespan to play the role that differential reproduction plays in direct natural selection accounts
findings.note: Offers non-historical and derived-function routes that complicate a strictly etiological sorting of organisms from watches and from trained systems.

findings.position: The entry reports a debate over whether function accounts can handle malfunction, along with the proper-function / derived-function machinery. This bears on whether unintended dispositions count as functions or malfunctions on an etiological reading. It does not treat unintended or misaligned outputs of designed systems.
findings.quote: Davies (2001) argues that the natural selection accounts are unable to provide an account of malfunction insofar as they individuate traits functionally
findings.note: Relevant analogy for sycophancy/reward hacking as function versus malfunction; no direct discussion.

nearest_positions: Etiological / selected-effects accounts of function, grounded in why a trait is there — Wright; Millikan; Neander; Wimsatt
Cummins-style causal-role functional analysis, which applies equally to artifacts and so does not sort organisms from watches — Cummins 1975; Lewens 2004
Organizational / self-maintenance accounts and Kant–Ginsborg natural purposiveness as non-historical ways of demarcating organisms — Mossio, Saborido & Moreno; Moreno & Mossio; Ginsborg 2004
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Gubelmann or any 'externally fixed goals' premise, LLMs or AI systems, sycophancy, reward hacking, and objective-based proxy accounts of goal-directedness. The entry does not discuss artifact teleology as grounded in designer-set objectives. It also does not discuss unintended output-time dispositions of trained systems or the placement of LLMs relative to organisms.

findings.position: The entry separates artifact functions, which rest on design or intention, from biological functions, which rest on selection history. It also requires that functions grounding original intentionality not depend on other intentional phenomena. This gives the thesis its organism/watch sorting criterion.
findings.who: Wright 1973 (artifact functions as purposive); Neander 1991 and Millikan 1989a (etiological theory); entry's own framing
findings.quote: the functions to which it appeals, as grounding original intentionality, cannot in turn depend on other intentional phenomena.
findings.note: Supplies the premise that externally fixed goals (designer-given) are not enough without a selection-history reading.

findings.position: On etiological theories a function is what an item was selected for, not what it is currently disposed to do, so a trait can have a function it fails to perform. Selection is not limited to natural selection: learning, conditioning, reward and neural selection also count. This gives the thesis a way to read training as a selection process and to separate trained-for function from output-time disposition.
findings.quote: Papineau (1984) speaks of learning and Dretske (1986) invokes functions that depend on recruitment by conditioning.
findings.note: Reward-based training is analogous to the entry's learning/conditioning selection; the entry does not apply this to artifacts or LLMs.

findings.position: Cases where the selected-for effect diverges from the intuitively represented content or behaviour. In the kimu case, Millikan's theory assigns content from the selected effect (snorf-free space), against the creature's apparent behavioural profile. This is a structural analogue to a proxy objective diverging from output-time dispositions.
findings.quote: On Millikan's theory, Bs mean snorf-free-space and there is no representation of red in a kimu's brain.
findings.note: A referee may cite the kimu as the existing debate about selection-grounded content diverging from disposition.

findings.position: Rival views hold that design functions or non-etiological functions can ground content, so an etiological reading is not required to sort organisms from artifacts. Shea allows design functions in place of stabilized functions. Nanay, Piccinini, Schroeder and Bauer combine teleosemantics with non-etiological accounts of function.
findings.quote: Shea allows that representational systems may have design functions instead of stabilized functions, so stabilization is not strictly necessary for representation
findings.note: Challenges the 'needs an etiological reading' step; the thesis must argue against these or restrict its claim.

findings.position: Objections to teleosemantics concerning what counts as a representational system. Swampman is the case with no selection history and so no function. Burge's liberalism objection says teleosemantics over-attributes representation to simple systems. Both bear on where an LLM would sit relative to organisms.
findings.quote: Swampman's component parts have no functions according to an etiological theory of function and so his "brain" states have no contents
findings.note: Frames the open placement question without answering it for trained artifacts.

nearest_positions: Etiological/selected-effects teleosemantics, extended to learning and conditioning as selection — Millikan, Papineau, Dretske, Neander, Garson
Non-etiological or design-function teleosemantics, on which an artifact's designed or modal function can ground content — Shea (design functions), Nanay, Piccinini
Liberalism and over-attribution worries, plus the Swampman/no-history problem — Burge, Artiga, Shea, Millikan
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Gubelmann, large language models, AI systems and machine learning training objectives; sycophancy, reward hacking and proxy-objective accounts; and any application of etiological functions to trained artifacts as opposed to organisms. The entry does not discuss whether training counts as selection that fixes goals, or whether artifacts with non-intentional selection histories qualify for content.

findings.position: AI's agents are defined by goals fixed externally by designers: intelligence as rationality, i.e. maximizing expected utility under a designer-specified performance measure U. This is the objective-based, externally fixed-goal picture the thesis targets. The entry offers no etiological reading of those goals.
findings.quote: A performance measure \(U\) evaluates this sequence; ... a perfectly rational agent can be taken to be the function \(f_{opt}\) which produces the maximum expected utility in the environment under consideration.
findings.note: Names the objective-based account whose goal-fixing the thesis would reread etiologically; does not address the etiological question.

findings.position: The entry's reinforcement-learning discussion supplies a basis for the thesis: the machine learns from occasional rewards and punishments, so the dispositions it ends up with are shaped by a training history, not read off the stated objective. The entry does not mention reward hacking or sycophancy.
findings.who: Entry's own exposition of reinforcement learning; Sutton & Barto (1998)
findings.quote: only occasionally receives feedback on its behavior in the form of rewards or punishments. The machine has to learn to behave rationally from this feedback.
findings.note: Gives a hook for output-time dispositions arising from the learning history rather than from a designer-fixed goal.

findings.position: Adversarial inputs show a gap between benchmark performance (the optimized objective) and real-world behavior, which is a mild precedent for unintended learned dispositions.
findings.who: Szegedy et al. 2014, as reported by the entry
findings.quote: has raised doubts about how well performance on benchmarks can translate into performance in real-world systems with sensory noise
findings.note: Analogous gap between the training objective and the resulting dispositions; not about sycophancy.

findings.position: The entry says machine ethics must worry about unintended consequences of codes and their representations, and the artifact-versus-animal contrast is its own framing. Neither is an etiological account of goals.
findings.who: Moral AI (Bringsjord et al.); entry's framing that AI aims to build 'artificial animals'
findings.quote: making sure that the moral code and its representation do not lead to unintended consequences
findings.note: Unintended consequences are raised, but only for engineered moral codes.

findings.position: The entry treats the question of whether artifacts reach animal- or person-level status as a goal and as a contested philosophical matter (strong vs. weak AI, Chinese Room). That is a different axis from the thesis's organism/watch sorting.
findings.quote: The ultimate goal of AI (which we are very far from achieving) is to build a person, or, more humbly, an animal.
findings.note: Organism-vs-artifact status is framed through mentality and personhood, not through the origin of goals.

nearest_positions: Intelligence as rationality / bounded optimality: agents maximize expected utility under a designer-specified performance measure — Russell; Russell & Norvig
Reinforcement learning: behavior shaped by occasional reward/punishment feedback, not an explicit specified function — Sutton & Barto, as reported
Strong vs. weak AI and the question whether artifacts can reach animal/person level — Haugeland, Charniak & McDermott; Searle (Chinese Room)
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Gubelmann or any 'externally fixed goals' premise; etiological or teleosemantic accounts of goals or function (selection history vs. design history) that would sort organisms from watches; sycophancy, reward hacking, specification gaming; large language models and their standing relative to organisms. The entry predates the LLM era and has no discussion of these topics.

theses: Gubelmann's 'externally fixed goals' premise needs an etiological reading to sort organisms from watches. On that reading, unintended output-time dispositions such as sycophancy and reward hacking strain objective-based proxy accounts. LLMs' placement relative to organisms is left open.
